query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

Own digest: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy transition-metal carbides be designed to exhibit tunable plasmonic properties in the near-IR to visible range while maintaining high thermal stability and mechanical hardness?. System: High-entropy transition-metal carbides (PHECs), specifically the archetype HfTa4C5 and a set of 14 six-element alloys (Carbon + 5 transition metals from groups 4, 5, and 6: Ti, Zr, Hf, V, Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, W). Processing: Computational: High-throughput disorder modeling using the Partial Occupation (POCC) method within the AFLOW framework to generate Boltzmann ensembles of superlattices, followed by time-dependent density-functional perturbation theory (TD-DFPT) calculations using VASP and turboEELS. Experimental: Ball-milling of TaC and HfC powders (4:1 ratio) followed by Field Assisted Sintering Technology (FAST) at 2100–2400 °C, 40–55 MPa, and 30–40 min hold times.. Test conditions: Computational: Optical limit (q=0) and varying transferred momentum (q); temperatures up to 1500 K. Experimental: Electron-energy
